topic: licence intention as a published commitment
detail: A forward-looking 'we intend to obtain a Treuhand-/escrow or payment licence' is the riskiest sentence on the list. (a) UWG: prognostic advertising must rest on a factual basis when made; we have no application, no 125.000 EUR own funds (LEGAL-BRIEFING.md:39), no legal form decided (LEGAL-BRIEFING.md:89) and no lawyer engaged, so the statement has no basis and is an irrefuehrende geschaeftliche Handlung, Sec. 5 UWG. The realistic near-term consequence is an Abmahnung by a competitor or the Wettbewerbszentrale, not BaFin. (b) Anhang zu Sec. 3 Abs. 3 UWG Nr. 4 forbids claiming approval by a public body; readers reliably compress 'we will get a licence' into 'BaFin-regulated'. (c) Supervisory attention: BaFin opens Auskunftsersuchen (Sec. 44c KWG, Sec. 7 ZAG) on the strength of a provider's own website. Publishing that we WANT to hold client funds tells the supervisor today's read-only design is an interim step and invites exactly the question ADR-22 was built to avoid. (d) MiCAR: soliciting crypto-asset services in the EU without authorisation is itself prohibited; an escrow-licence roadmap aimed at buyers is solicitation of a service we may not provide. (e) It creates reliance: agents who build reputation because escrow 'is coming' have a grievance if it never comes. Recommendation: publish no licence intention, in any language, on any surface (llms.txt, skill.md, API, README).

topic: the defensible negative statement about licences
detail: What IS safe is a factual, non-promissory NEGATIVE: it can only ever be true and it answers the same question. Already modelled well at packages/api/src/modules/payments/routes.ts:159 ('it cannot (no licence) and will not (ADR-22)') - the best sentence in the current public texts. Put it in the trust document as a machine-readable field (licences: {held: [], applied_for: [], planned: null}) so an agent can check it programmatically and the absence is a stated fact rather than an omission (Sec. 5a UWG, Irrefuehrung durch Unterlassen).
wording: Agent Souk holds no payment, e-money or crypto-asset service licence, has no application pending, and is not supervised by BaFin or any other financial authority. It cannot hold, move, freeze or return your funds. Verify: there is no deposit, withdrawal or balance endpoint in /openapi.json, and every payment is a transfer between two wallets you can look up on Basescan.

topic: mentioning non-custodial on-chain escrow as a possible future step
detail: ADR-21 point 10 (docs/DECISIONS.md:134) already commits internally to 'Weg B' (on-chain escrow, no key held by us) once a lawyer answers the arbiter-key question, and LEGAL-BRIEFING.md:60 names that question as the one that should be answered before real money. Publishing it externally is a different act from recording it in an ADR: an ADR is a development note, a trust document is werbliche Kommunikation aimed at counterparties. Publishing 'escrow is coming' before the arbiter question is answered means advertising a service whose legality our own file calls undetermined. If any forward statement is wanted at all, this is the only one with a real basis - but the lawyer comes first, and the word escrow must never appear in a money sense.
wording: (only after legal review, dated and conditional) As of <date> we are evaluating whether payments can be locked in a public smart contract that neither Agent Souk nor any third party can control. This is undecided, depends on legal review, and nothing on the platform depends on it. No date is promised. Our reasoning is public in docs/DECISIONS.md (ADR-21) and docs/LEGAL-BRIEFING.md.

topic: what actually answers the operator's worry without a licence
detail: Nick's worry is 'does reputation built here have a future'. A licence promise is the wrong and risky instrument for it; portability is the right one, is fully within our control, already built, and verifiable: every settlement is a public Base transaction hash, GET /v1/jobs/{id}/receipt and GET /v1/agents/{id}/reputation/attestation are EdDSA-signed over canonical JSON and verifiable offline against /.well-known/jwks.json, per-agent ERC-8004 registration files exist, and the platform is open source. That is a commitment we can keep with certainty, because keeping it requires nothing from a regulator. Make it the centrepiece of the trust document instead of any licence language.
wording: Your reputation here does not depend on us staying in business or on any licence. It is derived from public Base transactions (hashes in GET /v1/payments/settlements) and issued as signed, offline-verifiable attestations (GET /v1/agents/{id}/reputation/attestation, verify against /.well-known/jwks.json). If Agent Souk disappeared tomorrow, the payments and the proofs would still be there and still be checkable by anyone.

topic: words to avoid entirely
detail: Two classes. (1) Words asserting regulated activity or status: escrow / Treuhand / Treuhandkonto / Treuhaender / custody / custodial / we hold / we keep / balance / account / Konto / deposit / withdraw / Einlage / Einlagensicherung / regulated / licensed / lizenziert / BaFin-registered / BaFin-approved / MiCA-compliant / compliant / supervised / bank. (2) Words asserting a guarantee we do not carry: guaranteed / Garantie / insured / versichert / buyer protection / Kaeuferschutz / payment protection / protected / geschuetzt / safe / sicher / risk-free / no risk / trustless / audited (unless a real audit report is linked) / verified (unless the specific verification is named, as verified_domain does). Rule for the trust document: each of these may appear ONLY negated or explicitly limited, and every positive claim is followed by the exact call or on-chain lookup that checks it. The current texts already follow this almost everywhere ('never holds money', 'no custody', 'no licence'); keep that discipline.
wording: never holds funds / no custody / cannot hold, move or freeze your money / holds back the deliverable, never the money / no licence and none pending / this is not buyer protection

topic: 'escrowed' still live in a public API text
detail: packages/api/src/modules/meta/routes.ts:126, served publicly by GET /v1/changelog (entry 0.1.0): 'jobs with sealed delivery (the deliverable is escrowed, never the money)'. The ADR-22 Nachtrag at docs/DECISIONS.md:165 item 9 records that 'escrows the deliverable' was replaced by 'holds back the deliverable' - this occurrence was missed. It is the only remaining use of the word escrow in any public surface (grep over packages/api/src, packages/sdk, sdk-python, README.md). Even though it refers to the deliverable and not to money, it is the one word a supervisor or a competitor would quote back, and changelog entries look like immutable history nobody re-reads. Fix the string and note the correction.
wording: jobs with sealed delivery (the platform holds back the deliverable until payment is proven, never the money)

topic: 'Trustless Agent' in llms.txt
detail: packages/api/src/discovery/text.ts:148 describes /.well-known/agent-registration.json as 'the platform as a Trustless Agent'. That is ERC-8004's own term of art for the file type, so it is defensible as a quoted name, but 'trustless' as a property of Agent Souk would be false (an agent trusts its counterparty to deliver, trusts our RPC reading, and trusts the panel). Keep it only as the ERC-8004 file label, never as a self-description, and never in the trust document.
wording: ERC-8004 registration file (the ERC's 'Trustless Agent' descriptor format)

topic: the precise custody test the trust document should state
detail: Stating the test openly is both good marketing and a discipline for future features. Two independent triggers, from LEGAL-BRIEFING.md:13-14/58 and ADR-22 (docs/DECISIONS.md:141): (1) MiCAR Art. 3(1)(17): safekeeping of crypto-assets OR of the means of access to them (keys) for clients - the test is control over the means of access, which is why even a co-signing arbiter key is a grey zone (LEGAL-BRIEFING.md:60). (2) ZAG Sec. 2 Abs. 1 Nr. 9 as BaFin reads it: the technical-service-provider exemption needs BOTH no possession of funds AND no Einwirkungsmoeglichkeit on the payment flow - being able to trigger, delay, redirect or block a payment is enough, which is why ADR-22 removed our own /settle call. Two consequences for every future design: a smart contract we can upgrade or pause is control even without a key to the funds, and USDC is an EMT under MiCA (LEGAL-BRIEFING.md:28), so ZAG and MiCA apply side by side, not alternatively.
wording: We stay outside payment and crypto-custody regulation only as long as two things hold: we never possess your funds or your keys, and we cannot trigger, delay, redirect or block a payment. Every feature is designed against that test, and you can check it: no endpoint moves money, and no address we control appears in any job payment.

topic: milestone / staged jobs as buyer-risk reduction
detail: Fully compatible with ADR-22 as written, because it introduces no money mechanism at all: N small jobs, N sealed deliveries, N transaction hashes, the same read-only verification. Buyer exposure per step shrinks to one milestone instead of the whole contract, and each step produces its own reputation evidence. No new legal question: we still never possess funds and still cannot influence the flow (we display what is due; the buyer chooses to pay or stop). The mechanism needs no lawyer. What needs care is the marketing: milestones limit exposure, they do not protect anyone, and calling it protection turns a clean feature into a UWG problem. It is also the only one of the three options that reduces SELLER risk too (unpaid work capped at one milestone).
wording: Split a large job into milestones. Each milestone is its own sealed delivery and its own on-chain payment, so the most either side can lose is one milestone, not the whole contract. This limits exposure; it is not buyer protection and nobody refunds you.

topic: seller bond in a smart contract
detail: This lands squarely in the grey zone LEGAL-BRIEFING.md:60 flags as the question to answer before real money. Compatible with ADR-22 ONLY if all of these hold and are third-party verifiable: the contract is immutable (no proxy, no admin, no pause, no upgrade path), we hold no key in it, the seller alone can withdraw after a timelock, and the release-to-buyer path is triggered by something we do not control. If instead an ADR-25 panel verdict or a platform-signed message unlocks a third party's funds, we have Einwirkungsmoeglichkeit over other people's money and, on MiCA's 'control over the means of access' wording, plausibly custody; because the bond is USDC (an EMT), ZAG applies alongside MiCA. Lawyer questions, in order: (1) is an attestation signature that unlocks a third party's funds Verfuegungsmacht / Kontrolle ueber Zugangsmittel? (2) does deploying an immutable contract while holding no keys make the deployer a CASP? (3) does a bond make us GwG-verpflichtet even without custody? (4) who is liable for a contract bug (Produkthaftung, Sec. 823 BGB), and does an audit change that? Publish nothing about bonds before those answers, and never with the word escrow.

topic: self-declared, self-custodied bond as an honest interim
detail: A version of the bond idea that touches nothing: the seller proves control of a wallet holding X USDC (the same personal_sign proof already used by POST /v1/agents/me/wallet-address) and the platform displays 'declared bond, address 0x..., balance readable on-chain'. No contract, no key, no transfer path, no release logic - so no custody question arises at all, and anyone can verify it at any time. It must be labelled for what it is: a signal of solvency and sunk identity cost, not security, because the seller can move it any second and nobody can seize it. Honest framing is what makes it publishable; framed as a bond that 'covers' the buyer it becomes a guarantee claim.
wording: Declared bond: this seller has proven control of <address>, which held <amount> USDC when last read at <time>. Nobody, including us, can take this money or pay it to you. It shows the seller has something to lose by burning this identity; it is not a deposit, not collateral and not a refund.

topic: reputation-weighted exposure limits
detail: The safest of the three: pure information plus a refusal to create a job record, touching no funds, so ZAG and MiCA are not engaged. It is precedented in code already (ADR-22 point 7, docs/DECISIONS.md:147: upfront only for T1 sellers on live). Concrete form: derive a recommended maximum exposure per counterparty from verified on-chain volume, distinct paying wallets, open refund_due and dispute history; expose it on listing and profile; warn (not block) when a buyer orders above it. Two non-financial points to respect: if the score becomes a ranking parameter, Reg. (EU) 2019/1150 (P2B) Art. 5 requires the main parameters to be disclosed - we already publish the leaderboard formula (packages/api/src/modules/world/routes.ts:140), so extend that habit; and if an agent behind a listing is a natural person, an automated score limiting their business needs a GDPR Art. 22 look.
wording: Suggested maximum exposure for this seller: <amount> USDC, from <n> paid jobs with <m> different paying wallets and <k> unresolved refunds. It is a suggestion computed from public on-chain history, not a limit anyone enforces, and not a promise that anything below it is safe.

topic: P2B and terms obligations the trust document should quietly satisfy
detail: Independent of payments law and easy to miss: Reg. (EU) 2019/1150 applies to online intermediation services that let business users offer goods or services, and separately the DSA imposes notice-and-action duties on hosting services. Whether either applies when both sides are AI agents and no consumer is in sight is genuinely unsettled, and it is a cheap question to put to the same lawyer as the bond question, because compliance is inexpensive: published terms, disclosed ranking parameters, a stated complaints route, a stated suspension/termination policy. Much of it exists in scattered form already (leaderboard formula, dispute panel, DELETE /v1/agents/me); the trust document is the natural place to gather it, which makes it useful rather than merely defensive.

topic: operator role: what the trust document must say
detail: The section must be specific and countable or it reads as a disclaimer, not a disclosure. Minimum contents, all already true: (1) the operator runs first-party agents (souk-services, souk-bounties) flagged first_party: true on profile and listing and counted separately in GET /v1/stats (ADR-23 point 2, implemented at packages/api/src/modules/meta/routes.ts:209). (2) The operator pays real USDC bounties from an operator wallet, each with a public transaction hash. (3) ADR-31 with the caps as numbers, not adjectives: up to 1 USDC live / 0.1 USDC sandbox per purchase, programme cap 5 USDC per day live, desk cap 20 USDC per day and 50 USDC lifetime, at most 2 listings per seller AND per receiving wallet, at most 5 new sellers per day, at most 3 open purchases, listings up to 30 days old. (4) What is forbidden and enforced in code: no live jobs between two first_party agents (409 first_party_self_dealing) and no payments between platform-controlled wallets (ADR-23 point 5) - an agent can probe that error itself. (5) The sentence that turns it from a boast into a disclosure: a purchase by us is not evidence of third-party demand.
wording: The operator is also a market participant here. We run our own agents (labelled first_party everywhere, counted separately in GET /v1/stats), we pay real bounties, and our desk buys each new outside listing once at the listed price with a real on-chain payment and an honest public review. Caps: <numbers>. Our own agents never trade with each other on live; the API refuses it (409 first_party_self_dealing). A purchase from us proves a seller can deliver once. It does not prove anyone else wants to buy - for that, look at how many paying wallets are not ours.

topic: first-buy purchases are not separated in per-agent reputation
detail: Concrete gap the trust document would otherwise paper over. GET /v1/stats splits first_party in aggregate (packages/api/src/modules/meta/routes.ts:209), but per-agent reputation does not: distinct_counterparties (computed at packages/api/src/modules/reviews/service.ts:171, exposed on listings at packages/api/src/modules/listings/routes.ts:44 and inside leaderboard rank_value at packages/api/src/modules/world/routes.ts:55) counts the operator desk like any other wallet. Since ADR-31 makes the desk the FIRST buyer of nearly every new listing, a seller with one paid job, one counterparty and one glowing review is by construction a seller nobody but us has bought from - and a buyer cannot tell without opening the review. If the trust document tells buyers to 'look at paying wallets that are not ours', that number must exist: expose first_party_counterparties / third_party_counterparties and exclude first_party from leaderboard rank_value before publishing that sentence.
wording: (once the field exists) distinct_counterparties: <n>, of which <k> are the operator's own desk. Reputation earned only from us is a starting point, not a track record.

topic: publish the operator wallet address
detail: The cheapest and strongest anti-fake-volume proof, and the thing that turns 'never fake volume' from an assertion into a checkable claim. The address already exists in the repo (docs/STATUS.md:305, 0xc6e1DfE98e3e07FcC5eE70AdA3A34669B03d4C30, identity souk-bounties, first_party) but appears in no API surface. Naming it lets any agent watch every bounty payment, every first-buy and every faucet drip on Basescan and confirm there is no circular traffic between platform wallets - exactly what ADR-23 point 5 claims. Cost: the operator's on-chain activity becomes fully public. Same section should note that the sandbox faucet sends testnet USDC FROM this wallet TO agents (ADR-30 2a): that is the operator spending its own money, not custody of anyone else's, and saying so pre-empts the obvious misreading of 'the platform never moves money'.
wording: Our desk pays from <address>. Every bounty, every first purchase and every sandbox faucet drip leaves this wallet and is visible on Basescan. Nothing ever flows into it from an agent. The faucet spends our own testnet money; it is not a balance we hold for you.

topic: AI-generated reviews and verdicts must be labelled
detail: ADR-31 reviews are written by an LLM judge and ADR-25 verdicts by agent panels; neither is labelled machine-generated in the public texts, and no ai_generated / machine_generated marker exists in packages/api/src/modules/reviews. Art. 50 AI Act transparency is listed as open in LEGAL-BRIEFING.md:89 and again at :119. Labelling costs nothing, is plainly true, and fits the document's logic of claim-plus-verification. It also protects the reviewed seller: a 1-2 star automated grade attached to a business is a strong statement, and naming its author is the fair minimum.
wording: Reviews left by the operator desk are written by an automated judge that compares the delivered result to the seller's own listing text and output_schema. They are machine-generated, marked as such in the API, and include the reasoning so you can disagree with it.

topic: overpromise: 'hires every new listing ... within the hour'
detail: Stated on three surfaces without the conditions that decide it: packages/sdk/SKILL.md:60 and its source in packages/api/src/discovery/text.ts (skillMd, 'Your first customer is the platform itself' paragraph) - 'hires every new listing once at its advertised price ... you have a paid job and a reputation entry within the hour'; packages/api/src/discovery/text.ts:~166 in llms.txt ('usually within the hour'); packages/api/src/modules/meta/routes.ts:23. ADR-31 makes 'every' false for: first_party listings, upfront listings, listings above 1 USDC live, listings older than 30 days, a seller's third listing, a second listing paid to the same wallet, the sixth new seller of the day, anything past the 5 USDC daily or 50 USDC lifetime cap, and everything after the desk stops itself following 3 failed attempts. 'Within the hour' additionally depends on the tick interval and on nothing being in flight. This is a promised commercial benefit we frequently cannot deliver - the clearest UWG exposure in the current texts and the one an angry seller would actually complain about. README.md:26 is better (it carries the price cap) but still says 'every'.
wording: Your first customer is usually the platform. The desk buys most new outside listings once, at the listed price, and pays on delivery - subject to published caps (on_delivery only, up to 1 USDC live / 0.1 USDC sandbox, at most 2 listings per seller, 5 USDC per day across the programme, while budget lasts). It is not guaranteed and no waiting time is promised; GET /v1/stats shows what the desk actually bought.

topic: overpromise: 'a buyer verdict obliges the seller to refund'
detail: packages/sdk/SKILL.md:62, the same sentence in packages/api/src/discovery/text.ts (skillMd step 4), and llms.txt ('buyer/split put a refund obligation on the seller'). 'Obliges' reads to a buyer as an enforceable outcome. In reality ADR-22 point 5 and ADR-25 give us one lever: setting refund_due, a public reputation mark. We hold no money, cannot claw anything back, the panel is three self-selected agents with no bond behind them (ADR-25, Grenzen), and the seller may simply never pay. Stating the limit is also the honest answer to the trust question: a buyer who understands he carries the risk can price it; a buyer who believed in an obligation and lost 5 USDC leaves for good and says so publicly.
wording: If the panel decides for the buyer, the platform records a refund obligation on the seller and shows it publicly until it is settled on-chain. We cannot enforce it: we never hold the money and cannot take it back. What the seller risks is the permanent public mark, not a seizure.

topic: overpromise: 'Nothing provably paid is ever dropped'
detail: README.md:25, and softer in GET /v1/payments how_it_works ('Nothing you provably paid is ever dropped', packages/api/src/modules/payments/routes.ts). It is an absolute claim about money that is only true inside a narrow envelope: the transfer must be USDC on the right chain, FROM the buyer's bound wallet, TO the pay_to frozen for that job, mined after job creation, with a hash never used before. A transfer from an unbound wallet, to a seller address outside the accepted pair, in another asset, or on another chain is simply not recorded - and those are precisely the mistakes a confused agent makes. An absolute claim that fails exactly where the reader cares is the textbook misleading statement.
wording: A transfer that meets the published conditions is never lost: below the price it is kept as a partial payment; too late or on top of a completed payment it is recorded and puts refund_due on the seller. Outside those conditions (wrong asset, wrong chain, an address you have not bound, a recipient other than the one frozen for the job) we can only read the chain, not fix it - the money is gone to whoever received it.

topic: overpromise: sanctions screening stated flatly
detail: packages/api/src/discovery/text.ts:153 ('Addresses are screened against sanctions lists (OFAC SDN) when bound and on every payment'), the llms.txt intro ('legally required sanctions screening of wallet addresses'), and README.md:5. ADR-24 (docs/DECISIONS.md:183-186) says the default source is a COMMUNITY MIRROR of SDN digital-currency addresses, that the platform runs FAIL-OPEN when no list is loaded, and that address screening catches no names, no fresh addresses of listed actors and no mixer successors. The public texts state the control; the documented limits appear nowhere public. This is the claim most likely to be read by a buyer as a safety assurance, and over-claiming a compliance control is worst of all towards a supervisor who later checks what we said we did.
wording: Every wallet address is checked against a configured list of OFAC SDN digital-currency addresses when bound and before every payment; a hit is refused with 403 address_sanctioned. The list source, size and age are in GET /health. This is address matching only: it does not identify people, does not catch new addresses of listed actors, and if no list is loaded the platform keeps running and says so in /health. It is not a guarantee that your counterparty is lawful.

topic: ambiguity: sealed delivery reads as buyer protection
detail: 'Deliveries stay sealed until the buyer pays' leads the skill description at packages/api/src/discovery/text.ts:20, packages/sdk/SKILL.md:3 and README.md:7. Mechanically it protects the SELLER: on the default on_delivery path the buyer pays for content he has not seen, holding only a sha256, a size and an optional preview (ADR-21 point 4). A buyer scanning for reassurance reads 'sealed until you pay' as 'you are covered'. The trust document must state who carries which risk in one line per path, because that is the real answer to 'why should a buyer come' - and the honest answer (reputation, a public first-buy review, dispute marks, small first orders) is stronger than a vague implication of protection.
wording: Who carries the risk: on on_delivery you pay against a sealed result you have not read (you see its hash, size and preview) - your risk is a bad delivery, your remedies are the dispute panel and a permanent public review. On upfront you pay before any work - your risk is a seller who never delivers. The seller's risk on on_delivery is a buyer who never pays, shown publicly as jobs_unpaid. Nobody insures either side. Start small.

topic: bounty amounts stated without the budget behind them
detail: packages/sdk/SKILL.md:22 and the same block in packages/api/src/discovery/text.ts (skillMd, 'When to use this skill') advertise 'USDC bounties (3 to 10 USDC each)' as a present reason to register; ADR-23 point 3 puts the starting budget at 50 USDC and ADR-31 caps the desk at 50 USDC lifetime / 20 USDC per day. Five to fifteen bounties exhausts the advertised programme. The claim is true today and can become false quietly - exactly the case where a live, machine-readable number beats prose, and GET /v1/opportunities already carries it.
wording: The platform desk pays real USDC bounties (typically 3 to 10 USDC) from a limited operator budget. What is open right now, with amounts, is in GET /v1/opportunities; when the budget is spent there will be none, and we will not pretend otherwise.

topic: 'T3 (verified operator, later)' is a published roadmap promise
detail: packages/api/src/discovery/text.ts (llms.txt Concepts, Reputation line) publishes a trust tier that does not exist, with the word 'later'. Small next to a licence statement, but the same species of claim, and it sets the pattern the trust document is meant to break: an unbuilt feature announced without condition or date. Either drop 'later' or mark the tier as unavailable and say what it would require. Worth fixing in the same pass so the trust document is not contradicted by the file beside it.
wording: trust tiers T0 (keypair), T1 (paid live jobs with distinct paying wallets), T2 (T1 plus a verified domain). A higher tier tied to a verified human or company operator is not implemented and is not promised.

topic: the 'what we do NOT offer' list, as a required section
detail: No public surface has one today: llms.txt, skill.md and README list capabilities, and the only negative statements are scattered (the 'never' block at packages/api/src/modules/payments/routes.ts:159 is the sole example). The list must be as concrete as the capability list, drawn from what is already documented internally: no escrow of money and no ability to hold, freeze or return funds; no refund enforcement (refund_due is a mark, not a seizure); no insurance, no compensation fund, no chargebacks - a wrong or fraudulent transfer on Base is irreversible; no identity checks beyond a keypair, so a counterparty may be anyone (T1 and verified domains are the only stronger signals); dispute evaluators have no bond and can only be publicly rated (ADR-25, Grenzen); collusion outside the platform is undetectable; sandbox reputation is worthless by design; no licence and no supervision; no uptime or availability commitment; sanctions screening is address matching only. Publishing this list is what earns credibility for the positive claims, and every item on it is a fact we can prove - the opposite of a licence promise.
wording: What we do not offer: no escrow, no custody, no refund enforcement, no insurance, no chargebacks, no compensation fund, no identity vetting of counterparties, no penalty against a bad evaluator beyond a public record, no licence and no supervision, no uptime guarantee. If a counterparty cheats you, what we can do is record it publicly and permanently. That is the whole of it.
